source_document.body:
Nuclear power group AMPERA and Berto Acquisition Corp. jointly announced that the companies have entered into a definitive agreement for a business combination. The transaction implies an equity value for AMPERA of about $900 million on a pre-money equity.
AMPERA develops scalable power solutions for data center, defense, industrial, and maritime applications. As part of its business strategy, AMPERA is pursuing near-term commercial power generation using heat recovery and conventional fuels through its PowerNOW program, while simultaneously conducting longer-term development of advanced nuclear technology through its NuclearNEXT approach. AMPERA is combining advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence (AI), emerging quantum computing capabilities and next-generation energy technologies to develop reliable, highly efficient, factory-built power systems.
Berto is a publicly traded special purpose acquisition company. The group said that in connection with the business combination with AMPERA, it has entered into subscription agreements with certain institutional and accredited investors and strategic investors. Pursuant to the PIPE Subscription Agreements, Berto has agreed to issue and sell, and the subscribers agreed to subscribe for and purchase at closing, in a private placement, an aggregate of about $30 million of shares of Class A common stock of the post-merger combined company. The stock would be at a per share price equal to the price at which Berto’s public shares may be redeemed in connection with the business combination.
In addition to the PIPE financing, AMPERA has closed or received commitments for an additional $10 million in pre-transaction close equity and debt financing, bringing total capital commitments in excess of $40 million to date. The PIPE and the company’s existing investors include a leading AI data center equipment provider, one of the world’s largest quantum computing companies, a global maritime company, a U.S. defense contractor, and a Middle East industrial investor.
Berto and AMPERA are in discussions with a number of strategic and institutional investors regarding an additional $50 million to $100 million of PIPE capital. No definitive agreements have been signed for this additional capital, there is no assurance it will be raised, and the final amount may be higher or lower. Any additional capital would be incremental to the PIPE described above, and the transaction is not conditioned on its being raised.
The minimum cash condition in the transaction is set at the final PIPE raise amount. Accordingly, the transaction has no minimum cash condition above the amount of PIPE capital raised. For illustrative purposes, assuming $100 million of additional PIPE capital and no redemptions, gross capital available to AMPERA could exceed $450 million.
Upon closing, which is subject to approval by the stockholders of both AMPERA and Berto, receipt of required regulatory approvals and satisfaction or waiver of customary closing conditions, including the minimum cash condition described above, the combined company is expected to be named “AMPERA, Inc.” and is anticipated to list on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker symbol “AMPR,” subject to Nasdaq approval. The transaction is currently expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, although there can be no assurance regarding the timing or completion of the transaction. AMPERA intends to use expected proceeds from the transaction to fund its platform development and initial commercial scale-up, although the amount of proceeds available to the combined company will depend on, among other things, the level of redemptions by Berto’s shareholders and the total amount of financing raised.
“This transaction represents a defining milestone for AMPERA as we work to bring our advanced energy technologies to market,” said Brian Matthews, founder and CEO of AMPERA. “The rapid growth of AI infrastructure, data centers and industrial electrification is creating unprecedented demand for reliable, scalable power. Our PowerNOW platform is designed to address that demand through modular, high-efficiency power generation systems, with initial commercial deliveries targeted for 2027. In parallel, our NuclearNEXT program is advancing a fundamentally different approach to nuclear energy through a source-assisted, subcritical thorium architecture. We believe the combination of near-term commercial opportunities and longer-term nuclear innovation creates a compelling foundation for significant growth.”
AMPERA is developing a proprietary supercritical carbon dioxide (sCO 2 ) platform, the sPower power conversion cycle. The sPower technology is applicable across PowerNOW solutions, gas turbine bottoming cycles, industrial heat recovery and eventually NuclearNEXT.
AMPERA’s PowerNOW strategy provides fuel flexibility, efficiency and deployability advantages. The company currently plans to offer four configurations:
AMP-G7.5: AMPERA’s initial natural-gas-fired system utilizing sPower, targeting 7.5MW net electrical output and commercial production in Q4 2027.
AMP-G15: The next-generation evolution of AMP-G7.5, utilizing an enhanced sPower conversion system, targeting 15MW net electrical output.
sPower Heat Recovery: For use in industrial waste heat recovery, efficient bottoming cycle on gas turbines and other third-party heat sources.
PowerNOW Gas Turbine Variant: A higher-capacity configuration under development that integrates a conventional gas turbine with AMPERA’s proprietary sPower bottoming cycle, targeting up to 45MW total electrical output.
Under its NuclearNEXT strategy, AMPERA is developing the AMP-N15 to include a proprietary thorium-fueled, factory-sealed reactor based on a source-assisted subcritical architecture that targets 15MW net electrical output and an up-to 30-year core life with no routine refueling.
“We believe the combined entity will create significant value for shareholders by capturing what we see as a transformational market opportunity,” said Harry L. You, executive chairman of Berto Acquisition Corp. “AMPERA is uniquely positioned to lead the commercialization of near-term power production and the industrialization of nuclear energy at scale, serving the power demand from AI data centers, defense applications, maritime and industrial users. The AMPERA nuclear platform distinctively combines subcritical architecture, thorium fuel, no refueling, environmentally friendly non-water based cooling, and factory manufacturing in a single system. We have great confidence in the leadership of Brian Matthews and his team.”
Needham & Company, LLC is serving as financial advisor to AMPERA and as placement agent for the PIPE transaction. Sichenzia Ross Ference Carmel LLP is serving as legal advisor to AMPERA. White & Case LLP is serving as legal advisor to Berto.
—This content was contributed by the communications team for AMPERA .

View of a rig drilling the Makoko District in the Western Forelands. ( Image courtesy of Ivanhoe Mines’ Presentation )
By: Henry Lazenby November 20, 2026
Fewer mining projects moved closer to production in the quarter to Sept. 30, even as companies reported a record number of drill holes, S&P Global says.
Mining companies raised $9.81 billion (C$14.1 billion) in the quarter to Sept. 30, 28% less than the $13.6 billion they raised in the quarter to June 30, the consultant reported Wednesday. A drop in borrowing outweighed a rise in share sales.
“A shortage of metal does not begin when the market physically runs out of material,” Patricia Barreto, an associate director at S&P Global Energy, said during a webinar. “It begins several years earlier when good projects fail to move quickly enough from discovery to resource, from resource to feasibility and from feasibility into construction.”
S&P counted nine development milestones in the quarter to Sept. 30, down from 16 in the quarter to June 30 and 23 a year earlier. Five mines opened and construction began on two others. The drilling rebound could lead to more initial resource estimates and more projects advancing in 2027 if financing holds up, S&P said. The mining companies it tracks gained 6% in market value to $3.95 trillion, a record in its quarterly figures.
Gold leads drilling
Companies reported results from 18,474 drill holes, up 59% from the quarter to June 30 and the most in S&P’s series. The number of projects reporting results rose 36% to 718, the most since the quarter to March 31, 2023. Gold accounted for nearly six in 10. Silver accounted for 67 projects, more than double the number a year earlier. Copper rose 11% over the same period to 88 projects. Australia led with 230 projects, followed by Canada with 164 and the United States with 78.
The number of early-stage projects reporting drill results rose 51% from the quarter to June 30. They accounted for 42% of all projects reporting results. A separate S&P budget survey put global nonferrous exploration budgets at $16.5 billion this year, up a third, led by gold and copper. Canada’s budget rose 37% to $3.14 billion, largely on gold.
Drill results were the only component of S&P’s Pipeline Activity Index to improve. The index, which also tracks initial resources, financings and milestones, gained 5% from the quarter to June 30 but remained 14% below a year earlier. S&P counted 49 development milestones in the first nine months of 2026, close to the 51 it tracked in the same period last year.
From drill to mine
The only completed feasibility study in S&P’s tally came from Liberty Gold (TSX: LGD; US-OTC: LGDTF) at its Black Pine gold project in southeastern Idaho. The September study estimated a 16-year open-pit mine would cost $411 million to build. Liberty aims to finish detailed engineering in the third quarter of 2027 and start construction in the first half of 2028, subject to permits and a formal decision to build.
Miners announced eight initial resource estimates, down from 13 a year earlier. Two deposits accounted for most of the gold and copper in those estimates. At the Apollo deposit in Colombia, Collective Mining (TSX, Nasdaq: CNL) reported an indicated resource of 37 million tonnes at 1.38 grams gold per tonne for 1.64 million oz. and an inferred resource of 48.2 million tonnes at 1.6 grams for 2.47 million ounces. The estimate, effective Aug. 31, accounted for about two-thirds of the 6.2 million oz. of gold S&P tallied, including byproduct gold.
In Nevada, Lion Copper (CSE, Nasdaq: LCU) reported on Aug. 4 that the Bear deposit held an indicated resource of 1.06 billion tonnes at 0.29% copper for 3.04 million tonnes of the metal. An inferred resource of 1.77 billion tonnes at 0.22% contained 3.98 million tonnes. Bear accounted for about 91% of the 7.7 million tonnes of copper in the quarter’s initial estimates, including byproduct copper.
Equity overtakes debt
Debt financing fell 54% from the quarter to June 30, bringing total fundraising to its lowest level since the quarter to Dec. 31, 2024. Share sales accounted for 59% of the money miners raised, up from 36% the previous quarter. In September, the U.S. Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate by a quarter of a percentage point.
Generation Mining (TSX: GENM; US-OTC: GENMF) raised C$240 million through a bought deal and a private placement with Canada Growth Fund to help build its Marathon copper-palladium project in northwestern Ontario. Generation began construction in October.
Majors raised 65% less than in the quarter to June 30, while juniors raised 8% less. A rebound in financing by mid-tier miners lifted the combined total for juniors and mid-tiers by 14% to $7.05 billion. The number of significant financings for the two groups fell to 146 from 272 a year earlier.
Alcoa (NYSE: AA; ASX: AAI) raised $2.6 billion through two subsidiaries to help buy bauxite, alumina and aluminum assets from South32 (ASX, LSE: S32). The $1.5-billion bond issued by Alcoa subsidiary Alumina Pty Ltd. was the largest financing S&P tracked in the quarter. Mid-tier producer Wanguo Gold Group (HKEX: 3939) raised HK$5.5 billion (about $700 million) through convertible bonds to pursue gold mine acquisitions overseas.
Where capital went
Canadian projects drew the most financing at $1.77 billion. Financing for Latin American projects rose 56% from the quarter to June 30 to $1.63 billion. S&P’s regional tally excludes debt issues above $500 million.
S&P tracked 49 mining deals worth at least $5 million each. Gold accounted for 22 and copper for 16. Across all commodities, 37 deals involved assets that weren’t producing.
Investors favour producing mines and advanced projects, S&P Global Energy associate director Nick Trickett said. Further rate increases and swings in metal prices would leave juniors especially exposed as they try to raise money, he said.

8-Lug Pontiac Catalina 2+2 Is a One-Family Power Cruiser, Original 421 Pulls Like a Tug Boat
61 photos
Photo: YouTube/Chief Classics
How many gearheads stick with their car for more than six continuous decades? Most enthusiasts cycle through projects like socks, chasing the next distraction before the paint even cures. Yet once in a blue moon, a survivor surfaces after a lifetime under one family roof. Meet this Cameo Ivory-over-red 1965 Pontiac Catalina 2+2 hardtop, a Pacific Northwest time capsule recently revived for open-road duty by Jeff Herrick Jr. of Chief Classics.
According to the original paperwork and Pontiac Historical Services documents inside, this full-size Poncho boulevard bruiser was sold brand-new on August 23, 1965, at Chuck Gaines Pontiac in Auburn, Washington. The original buyer financed the $4,525 tab through 36 monthly payments of $100.
Its option list reads like a dream: bucket seats , center console, tilt column, wood-rimmed steering wheel, power steering, power brakes, Soft-Ray glass, VerbaPhonic reverb, and signature Kelsey-Hayes eight-lug wheels.
Remarkably, the car stayed in one family until bought from the original owner's son, retaining its Protect-O-Plate, an untouched eight-lug spare, and extra studded snow tires proving year-round duty. Receipts trace tires from 1987, a $1,870 Imron repaint in 1988, a 1989 transmission rebuild at 34,562 miles (with just over 50,000 showing now), a $362 cylinder-head rebuild in 2007, an alternator in 2008, and a final 2018 insurance slip marking its dormancy.
Photo: YouTube/Chief Classics To appreciate this full-size Pontiac with a sportscar middle name, rewind to the brand's rebellious peak. In 1963, a 421 Super Duty Tempest trounced Ferrari's V12 250 GTO at the Daytona 250 Challenge Cup, averaging 145 mph (233 kph). Riding that wave, John DeLorean's crew unleashed the midsize GTO for 1964 alongside a quieter companion: the Catalina 2+2 package, bringing bucket seats, console, heavy-duty suspension, and a standard 389-cubic-inch (6.4-liter) V8 with an optional 421.
For 1965, Pontiac stopped whispering and marketed the 2+2 as the GTO's big brother. It dropped "Catalina" from the exterior badges, added front-fender gills, pinstripes, and full-length trim, and promoted the 421-cubic-inch (6.9-liter) V8 to standard hardware.
Hardtop MSRPs started near $2,910, with convertibles around $3,200, squaring off directly against Chevrolet's 409- or 396-powered Impala SS (depending on which time of the model year we’re talking about), Ford's 427-optioned Galaxie 500XL, and Dodge's stylish Polara 500 packing 426 Wedge muscle.
Photo: YouTube/Chief Classics Every 1965 Catalina 2+2 packed serious Detroit torque. The base four-barrel 421, like this car's YH-code motor, made 338 hp (343 PS) and 459 lb-ft (622 Nm). Optioning Tri-Power carbs bumped output to 356 hp (361 PS) and 459 lb-ft, while the top-dog 421 H.O. Tri-Power unleashed 376 hp (381 PS) and 461 lb-ft (625 Nm). Transmission choices spanned a standard 3-speed manual, optional 4-speed , or 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic automatic.
That muscle sparked scandal in 1965 when Car and Driver pitted a 4,400-pound (2-ton) 376-hp 2+2 against a 3,430-pound (1.55-ton), 300-hp Ferrari 330 GT 2+2. Overcoming 3.42 gears against the Ferrari's 4.25 rear, the Poncho hit 60 mph (97 kph) in 3.9 seconds versus the Italian’s 6.3, and ran the quarter-mile in 13.8 seconds at 106 mph (171 kph), completely trouncing the Prancing Horse’s 14.6 at 97 mph (156 kph).
There was a rumor (that Pontiac never really bothered to clean off) that the 421 in that 2+2 was actually a 428, and that Royal Bobcat’s treatment had a lot to do with the Ferrari seeing its pompous horse badge finely sliced into cowboy flat iron steak. The only consolation the 330/GT 2+2 got from that bombardment was the track time attack run, where it finished in 2:00:85, just inching ahead the Catalina’s 2:01:33.
Photo: YouTube/Chief Classics Such scandalously devastation meant a lot of publicity, which in turn drove 2+2 production from 7,998 units in 1964 to an all-time peak of 11,521 in 1965, before sliding to 6,383 in 1966 and 1,768 in 1967. For 1965, Pontiac broke those 11,521 cars down by transmission—5,316 synchromesh manuals and 6,205 Turbo Hydra-Matic automatics—without publishing an official 2+2 engine-by-engine tally.
Still, every copy left with a 421, and just 1,082 manual WJ 421 H.O. blocks were cast across the whole lineup.
Pontiac boldly promoted the 2+2 to standalone model status for 1966, right as the GTO topped 96,000 sales and Chrysler's Street Hemi arrived. Demoted back to an option for 1967, neither fastback styling nor a new 428-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) V8—360 hp standard or 376 hp across 261 H.O. builds, 144 with 4-speeds—fended off the Firebird, Dodge’s Coronet R/T, or Shelby GT500.
Photo: YouTube/Chief Classics U.S. production ended after 1967, though Chevy-powered Canadian 2+2 models continued through 1970. That rarity makes Jeff Herrick Jr.'s Nebraska revival all the sweeter. Rolled off a Friday-night transport truck, the survivor revealed a crisp red Morrokide interior, solid undercoated floors, and its numbers-matching YH-code 421 with correct No. 76 heads and Carter four-barrel.
Astonishingly, it fired instantly on an August 2007 battery with nearly 40 PSI of oil pressure, though a maiden breakfast run exposed treacherously grabby front brakes determined to toss Jeff toward the windshield.
Up on the lift, pulling the prized eight-lug drums exposed the culprit: both front wheel cylinders were weeping brake fluid straight onto the shoes. Jeff installed new cylinders and shoes, bled the single-pot drum system, checked the open differential, and poured in high-zinc Valvoline VR1 20W-50 oil for the flat-tappet V8. A fresh battery, machine-polished chrome bumpers, and balanced GripMax wide-whitewall tires finally retired the cracking 1987 rubber for good.
Photo: YouTube/Chief Classics Next came chasing the sneaky gremlins that haunt dormant classics. Choppy, binding power steering disappeared once Jeff replaced two glazed, ancient belts. A phantom left blinker cured itself after reseating the horn cap and relay, while a 1965 dimmer mirror, tightened visors, and greased door hinges restored civility.
Dead taillights and brake lights proved trickiest, traced to a defective replacement headlight switch and fixed with an original 1965 unit from a parts car. With the blue coating scrubbed off its whitewalls and fresh 91-octane gas aboard, the big 2+2 reclaimed windy mid-November Nebraska roads like Lyndon Johnson was still in office.
Cruising smoothly at 55 to 65 mph (89 to 105 kph), the original 421 maintained 40 PSI of oil pressure below 175 degrees Fahrenheit (79 Celsius), steering with one finger and braking straight and true. Over 60 years after leaving Auburn, this one-family Pontiac proves true Pontiac iron is just as dependable and reliable as it was when John Z. DeLorean was riding the high-horse show in Michigan.

CACI’s SkyValor drone defense system uses long-range detection and a layered sensing architecture to expand the range at which drones can be identified and targeted. (Photo courtesy of CACI.)
Drone threats give defenders less time to determine intent and select the appropriate response to protect borders, military installations, and critical infrastructure with no/low collateral damage.
CACI International’s SkyValor next generation drone defense system is designed to expand that decision space through long-range detection and a layered architecture that combines radio frequency (RF) sensing, radar, electronic warfare, cellular detection, and electro-optical and infrared sensors. Breaking Defense talked about SkyValor with CACI’s CTO Jason Bales.
Breaking Defense: Before we get into the details of SkyValor, what threat scenarios is it designed to address, and why are these concerns more urgent now?
Bales: SkyValor builds on more than two decades of designing and deploying counter‑UAS systems worldwide. Over 300 fielded systems have informed our understanding of how drone threats evolve across national security missions, homeland defense, and critical infrastructure protection.
Jason Bales, CTO, CACI
We’ve taken that day‑to‑day operational insight and transformed it into a commercial offering purpose‑built for homeland and national security missions. Border defense is a major focus—tracking drones operating near or across national boundaries, as well as protecting critical infrastructure from incursions. Our long‑range detection gives operators the decision space to determine intent and escalate force appropriately across a rapidly shifting threat landscape.
Range is one of SkyValor’s attributes. Tell us about this.
SkyValor doesn’t just extend the detection envelope, it transforms the entire decision space. While most Group 1–3 systems spot a drone only one to five kilometers out, giving operators a frantic 10‑second window to react, SkyValor reaches an impressive 75 kilometers. That jump in range turns split‑second choices into a deliberate, 18‑ to 20‑minute tactical advantage, giving operators the breathing room to read intent, weigh options, and apply precisely the right level of force.
SkyValor can spot Group 1-3 drones at up to 75 kilometers, giving operators much more time to react. (Photo courtesy of CACI.)
Describe SkyValor and its components, and where it fits within a broader counter-UAS architecture.
It’s a multi‑layered architecture built for a fast‑moving threat. Our RF heritage enables long‑range detection, signal analysis, and the ability to break into a drone’s communications and create cyber effects—and to apply those effects to steer or take over the platform. The system can also jam broadly when confronting swarms. Our RF and EW capabilities are built in‑house, and we integrate commercial radar for added range and precision. A key differentiator is our cellular‑network technology, which detects and mitigates drones using cellular links, alongside EO/IR sensors and integration with kinetic interceptors.
Tell us about your non-kinetic defeat options.
Non‑kinetic effects allow us to neutralize a drone with almost surgical precision. Instead of relying on expensive interceptors that may require multiple shots, we use software‑driven energy effects that deliver low or no collateral damage and provide an essentially unlimited magazine. It’s the difference between having to physically remove a threat and being able to outthink it by using the system’s intelligence to quietly and efficiently disable or redirect a platform long before it becomes a problem. Kinetic tools certainly have their place, but SkyValor’s long‑range detection lets operators be deliberate rather than reactive. When you have minutes instead of seconds, you can choose the right level of force instead of defaulting to the most aggressive one. That measured escalation preserves valuable interceptors for situations where they’re truly needed.
How does being software-defined change the equation?
Being software‑defined changes the entire equation. It means our non‑kinetic effects aren’t fixed – they evolve. At a recent event, a drone operator tried [JB1] to slip past us by altering their waveform. In half an hour, we pushed a new update across the system and reasserted control. That agility is a hallmark of SkyValor: rather than chasing the threat, we stay ahead of it. The platform adapts in real time, letting operators counter new behaviors as soon as they appear.
What did the recent testing of SkyValor at Yuma and the southern border demonstrate?
Our recent work with JIATF-401 at Yuma and along the southern border was a real proving ground. It combined controlled test runs with unpredictable, real‑world encounters—short‑range pop‑ups, long‑range crossings, low‑altitude skimmers, and drones using a mix of communication links. Every time the environment changed, SkyValor kept pace. Those trials didn’t just validate performance metrics; they demonstrated the system’s ability to adapt to a living, evolving threat landscape.
What does CACI uniquely contribute in detection, tracking, processing, and non-kinetic defeat?
We designed SkyValor to operate autonomously from day one. That means it can collect, detect, track, and relay information without waiting for human intervention—all while feeding curated, AI‑filtered insights back to operators. The autonomy isn’t about removing humans from the equation; it’s about giving them cleaner, more actionable intelligence. When the system is doing the heavy lifting behind the scenes, operators can focus on making confident, well‑timed decisions in a compressed battlespace.
What real-world scenarios best illustrate where SkyValor adds the most value?
Border protection is a prime example. You want to know when a drone is approaching long before it crosses the line, and SkyValor gives you that early warning, turning a few frantic seconds into a structured decision window. By: Staff Writer November 20, 2026
Angola plans to pay about $180 million (C$258 million) for a 10% stake in De Beers , the head of state diamond miner Endiama said, as African producers seek greater control over the industry.
Endiama CEO José Manuel Augusto Ganga Júnior disclosed the amount on Friday, according to Reuters . The report didn’t detail how the investment would be structured.
The announcement comes as Botswana backs a takeover proposal from the Gareth Penny-led Global Diamond Consortium (GDC), while seeking to double its own holding in De Beers from 15% to 30%.
The negotiations could reshape ownership of one of the world’s best-known diamond companies, giving producing nations a larger stake in the business even as weak natural diamond demand and competition from laboratory-grown stones undermine its value.
Ownership questions
Anglo American (LSE: AAL) put De Beers up for sale in 2024 as part of a broader restructuring. The mining group holds 85% of the diamond company, with Botswana owning the remainder.
Botswana President Duma Boko announced on Nov. 9 that his government had selected GDC as its preferred bidder for Anglo American’s controlling interest. Anglo said it was still working with the governments and consortium towards binding transaction documents, Reuters reported.
In a Nov. 12 statement, Angola’s mining ministry outlined its participation in the proposed acquisition alongside GDC, Botswana, Namibia and Oman. It did not disclose the ownership allocation among the participants.
On a simple proportional basis, $180 million for 10% would imply an equity value of $1.8 billion for De Beers. That calculation doesn’t establish an agreed transaction valuation because the structure of Angola’s investment hasn’t been disclosed.
Rapaport News reported on Nov. 10, citing a source, that GDC’s offer included $750 million up front and $250 million in deferred payments to Anglo, while a $500-million capital injection into De Beers remained under discussion. Those terms cannot be compared directly with Angola’s proposed investment without knowing what each amount covers.
African ambitions
According to Angola’s ministry, the proposed shareholding would give the country a voice in De Beers’ strategy and help develop domestic diamond cutting, polishing and marketing.
Ganga Júnior said Angola’s proposed investment remained worthwhile despite the downturn in gem prices, Reuters reported. De Beers already explores in Angola with Endiama; the partners announced the discovery of a new kimberlite field in August 2025.
Endiama’s CEO spoke after the inauguration of Angola’s first gold refinery in Viana, Luanda. Built and financed by Endiama, the facility has a design capacity of up to 25 kilograms of gold a day, according to the government. Print

Ukrainian drone manufacturer Skyfall shows its Vampire unmanned system at the Dubai Airshow on Nov. 19, 2025. (Daniel Woolfolk / Breaking Defense)
WASHINGTON — American autonomous software firm Auterion and Ukrainian drone producer Skyfall plan to form a joint venture to “manufacture drones for Ukraine at high volume in a new factory in Germany,” Auterion announced today.
The new venture, called Skyfall X Auterion, “is being established under the auspices of the official ‘Build with Ukraine’ defense cooperation framework,” the announcement said.
According to Auterion, “initial production” by the joint venture will “focus on the Shrike FPV platform” and is expected to later expand to Skyfall interceptors as well as middle- and deep-strike systems. “Every drone combines a Skyfall airframe with Auterion avionics” as well as Auterion’s operating system, the company said.
Auterion and Skyfall previously partnered for drone production for Ukraine, but Auterion said today that a German factory in particular “adds production capacity outside the range of air strikes, while maintaining a knowledge link and short innovation cycle available to Skyfall’s engineers.
“Feedback from units at the front reaches those engineers every week and goes straight into the German line,” the company said.
Auterion, which is based in Munich as well as the US, said the agreement was inked during the German-Ukrainian Economic Forum today, and Reuters reported that the German government would provide funding for the new factory and for drone orders. Citing an industry official, the newswire reported the funding would be in the range of hundreds of millions of euros first to provide drones to Ukraine and then to the German armed forces.
“SkyFall and Auterion have put more than 50,000 drones into the hands of Ukrainian units with advanced terminal guidance and target detection” Lorenz Meier, founder and CEO of Auterion, said in the announcement. “A factory in Germany gives German forces a domestic source for the same drones Ukrainian units rely on every week.”

source_document.body:
Zim Integrated Shipping Services reported third-quarter net income of $830 million, up from $123 million a year earlier, as sharply higher freight rates lifted revenue and prompted another increase in its full-year earnings forecast.
The Haifa, Israel-based container carrier (NYSE: ZIM ) said that revenue rose 53% to $2.71 billion in the three months ended Sept. 30. Diluted earnings per share increased to $6.88 from $1.02.
Average freight rates climbed 55% year over year to $2,480 per twenty-foot equivalent unit , or TEU, while cargo volume increased 4% to 962,000 TEUs, as pricing, rather than volume growth, provided the main lift to quarterly revenue.
Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization increased 124% to $1.33 billion. Adjusted operating earnings, or EBIT, reached $993 million, compared with $260 million a year earlier, while the adjusted EBIT margin expanded to 37% from 15%.
“By keeping our network agile and focusing on premium, profitable trades, we are supporting our customers and positioning ZIM for further growth,” President and Chief Executive Chen Lichtenstein said in the earnings release.
Rates remained unusually strong on both coasts, Lichtenstein said on a call with analysts, noting Asia-U.S. West Coast and East Coast market conditions had not experienced the typical late-summer decline seen in prior years. He linked the broader freight-rate strength to port congestion, particularly in China, and disruptions affecting major shipping passages.
“We do see some softening in recent weeks,” he said, attributing it to customers delaying orders and avoiding bringing products into the U.S. around Christmas and year-end. “There is an expectation that the market will pick up again in January before the Chinese New Year,” he added.
Lichtenstein said e-commerce was feeding demand for expedited trans-Pacific services, while Zim had established a task force focused on suppliers serving AI and data centers. He also identified opportunities to shift cargo from airfreight to expedited ocean shipping.
Management said freight forwarders handle much of the high-value cargo Zim targets and had paid higher average rates than direct cargo owners on both Asia-U.S. coasts in each of the past three years. Lichtenstein also emphasized limiting annual contract volumes to preserve pricing flexibility.
Zim now expects full-year adjusted EBITDA of $3.3 billion to $3.5 billion and adjusted EBIT of $2 billion to $2.2 billion. Its previous ranges were $2.7 billion to $3 billion and $1.4 billion to $1.7 billion, respectively.
The increase follows Zim’s October guidance upgrade, when it cited strong market demand and favorable freight-rate momentum.
The stronger results also echo Hapag-Lloyd’s ( HLAG.DE ) third-quarter performance, which showed higher freight rates driving a sharp profit increase despite broadly unchanged cargo volumes.
Zim’s reported earnings benefited from a non-cash reversal of an earlier asset impairment. Adjusted net income, which excludes that benefit and acquisition-related costs, totaled $717 million, up from $124 million a year earlier. The impairment reversal added $155 million after tax to reported profit, while acquisition-related costs totaled $41 million after tax.
Zim generated $1.24 billion in operating cash flow and $1.22 billion in free cash flow during the quarter. Net debt, which includes lease liabilities, fell to $1.86 billion at Sept. 30 from $2.77 billion at June 30.
The board declared a dividend of $2.01 per share, or approximately $243 million, representing about 30% of aggregate net income for the first nine months of 2026.
For the first nine months, revenue increased to $5.89 billion from $5.42 billion, while net income rose to $808 million from $443 million. Cargo volume slipped to 2.75 million TEUs from 2.765 million.
New services as takeover review continues
Zim said it launched ZX3, its third premium expedited Asia-U.S. West Coast service, and Falcon, offering faster transit times from China to Argentina and southern Brazil. The carrier currently operates 112 containerships with combined capacity of approximately 703,000 TEUs, along with 13 car carriers.
Meanwhile, Hapag-Lloyd’s proposed acquisition of Zim for $35 per share in cash remains subject to regulatory approvals, including Israel’s consent under its special state share. Zim said the original application to the Israeli government was terminated and Hapag-Lloyd intends to submit a new application soon.
FreightWaves previously reported that Israel required a new review of the takeover after objections to the original transaction structure prompted a revised proposal.
Zim now says the transaction is targeted to close in the first quarter of 2027. The carriers remain separate, independent companies until closing.
Why it matters: For shippers, the launch of another expedited Asia-U.S. West Coast service adds a premium routing option, while the upgraded outlook signals management expects a stronger full-year financial result.

Honda Is Recalling the S2000 Roadster for Fuel Flange Joint Leak Risk
7 photos
Photo: Honda / edited
Honda has identified a rather worrying issue affecting one of the company's most celebrated production models. According to American Honda Motor, an estimated 16,387 examples of the S2K may feature replacement fuel flange joints without the brazing material designed to secure the joint-to-flange connection.
AHM claims the subject parts could loosen due to vibration, separate completely, allowing dinosaur juice to escape. This could either starve the engine of gasoline, bringing the two-seat roadster to an unexpected stop. Warnings include fuel odor and leakage, reduced acceleration response, misfiring, stalling, and the failure to restart. Sanoh Industrial is the supplier of the subject component.
Part number 16623-PCX-003 is also listed in the recall documentation, where American Honda Motor explains that a customer in Japan prompted the Japanese automaker to investigate. Said customer experienced symptoms in November 2025. Two months later, a used vehicle was sourced for testing.
The Japanese automaker conducted tests and analyzed the concern through May 2026. A brazing identification method for potentially affected components was developed in July 2026. Between August and October, the company investigated the potentially affected S2000 population, including cars potentially repaired with the defective assembly.
Thankfully for everyone, American Honda Motor has not received any warranty claims or field reports potentially related to the described concern. Referred to as 26V749 by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, this recall involves 2004 and 2005 models.
Photo: Honda That means all suspect vehicles are AP2s, namely the S2000 with the larger-displacement engine that is better in terms of low- and mid-range torque. The 2.2-liter mill doesn't rev as high as the 2.0-liter screamer of the AP1, but nevertheless, the AP2 prides itself on shorter lower gears, a taller sixth, carbon-fiber synchros, revised suspension, and larger wheels.
Honda further worked its magic in terms of styling, updating both the front and rear bumpers, the headlights, taillights, and exhaust finishers. Objectively, the AP2 is the better all-around package while the AP1 is the more intense, purer sports car. Also worth noting, the subject 2004 and 2005 models are AP2s with a traditional cable throttle and no traction control.
Starting with model year 2026, the US-market S2K switched to an electronic throttle control system that still uses a cable to connect the loud pedal to the sensor. Vehicle Stability Assist, meanwhile, combines stability and traction control. As you'd expect from such a magnificent sports car, VSA can be turned off.
Honda ultimately identified 67 replacement parts that its supplier manufactured without the required brazing operation, specifically the process where two or more metal components are joined by melting a filler metal into the joint. Said material reinforces the joint-to-flange connection, but due to the potential lack of material, the press-fit connection is vulnerable to loosening and separation.
Subject vehicles were produced between April 14, 2003, and September 21, 2005. The S2000 was produced at the Takanezawa and Suzuka plants through August 2009, with Suzuka taking over from Takanezawa in May 2004. Just under 110,700 units were produced in total, and over half were sent to the US market. Per the Part 573 safety recall report, owners will be notified in January 2027.

Stuart Smith (right), SRK Consulting’s chief operating officer for North America, in conversation with The Northern Miner video host Devan Murugan.
By: Northern Miner Staff November 20, 2026
Longer permitting timelines and construction cost overruns are pushing mining companies towards acquisitions, but buying an operating mine brings its own liabilities, says Stuart Smith, SRK Consulting’s chief operating officer for North America.
Smith spoke with The Northern Miner about the forces shaping mining mergers and acquisitions, opportunities for juniors and why technical due diligence matters when buyers weigh growth against risk.
The Northern Miner: What’s changed in mining M&A over the past five years?
Stuart Smith: First of all is the build versus buy decision. Build seems to be losing to buy. Permitting timelines are becoming longer in a number of jurisdictions. We see capital cost overruns hitting the headlines and producing or near producing assets seem to be garnering more attention.
Secondly, we’re seeing new entrants in terms of capital available to people who are trying to move projects forward, whether that’s streaming companies being more active in the market, state-backed lending institutions, or even equity institutions. And finally, OEMs [original equipment manufacturers] with vertical integration into their battery supply chains.
Finally, and perhaps not new, but more important than ever, is timing and discipline still matter. You’re seeing transactions in price environments that, in hindsight, look good or bad, depending on the time of the transaction.
TNM: Why does gold generate so many deals, while copper attracts larger investments?
SS: Gold’s historically a more fragmented market. You see record prices creating megadeals, but even if those do occur, you see spinoffs of tier two or non-core assets kind of perpetuating that fragmentation.
In terms of the copper space, certainly majors are going after large tier one long-life assets. That’s really supported by this longstanding theme of electrification and the supply-demand imbalance that a lot of people are predicting in the future.
TNM: What risks come with buying an operating mine?
SS: Well, we’re certainly seeing clients lean to producing assets, or at least have some form of near producing criteria, whether that be a completed PFS [prefeasibility study], FS [feasibility study], or permits in hand. It’s a bit of a double-edged sword in our view.
With a project, you can engineer the risks out, but when you buy a producing asset, you’re inheriting risks, whether that’s water treatment, geochemistry issues, tailings, or closure.
This is where when looking at producing assets, due diligence really earns its keep.
TNM: Where does that leave junior exploration companies?
SS: I personally think that there’s still plenty of place for juniors in our market. M&A moves assets around, but it doesn’t create them.
The other thing that we see is these post-merger spinoff assets can create a world in which juniors can acquire a quite good quality asset and build a portfolio around it. From our perspective, what really matters here is juniors need to be in a place where they have data and a story of the asset that stands up to due diligence.
TNM: Will investors pay more for assets in Canada and Australia?
SS: In short, yes. Australia and Canada are blessed geologically as well, so there’s certainly more assets available.
But getting those assets through permitting also provides a premium in those jurisdictions where it’s been historically difficult sometimes to get assets all the way to production. There are risks associated with other jurisdictions, whether you see what happened in Panama or in Mali, which are these low likelihood, high consequence risks that are hard to price in, but a safe jurisdiction certainly looks good.
But the final thing I’ll say about that is that even if you’re in a good jurisdiction, a good jurisdiction doesn’t fix a poor asset.
TNM: How do Chinese buyers approach acquisitions differently?
SS: Well, Chinese firms can look at deals differently. They’re taking the approach of a longer time horizon. Supply security is key. They’re able to act counter-cyclically, which we can’t see out of a number of the Western firms, where they can make deals that in hindsight look very well timed.
The issue that they’re facing now is they’re limited by a number of things like foreign investment reviews in some jurisdictions, and this is pushing them into areas like Africa and Latin America, as you suggest, where competition’s becoming quite hot for good assets.
The final thing I’ll say there is I think the narrative of Chinese firms having not as strong ESG [environmental, social and governance] credentials as the West is dying out and Western firms no longer automatically have the upper hand in that area.
TNM: How does SRK bring technical expertise and local knowledge together?
SS: SRK looks at the entire mining lifecycle through exploration, geology, mining environment, all the way through to closure.
And by taking that holistic picture, we’re able to understand the true picture of the asset across all the disciplines; not only from a technical basis, but we have people around the world in all the major mining jurisdictions and we can really bring that local understanding, but also a global context.
TNM: How do you help clients assess risk in a volatile market?
SS: Risk tolerance is really going to come down to the acquirer, the buyer and their unique situation. I think where we like to set ourselves apart is being able to understand the technical fundamentals of the asset and link that to the business transaction that’s being contemplated.
And so we’re not just looking at the pure technical, but also the context of our client and that’s really the fundamentals that matter regardless of the environment.
TNM: Where do you see the next opportunities in mining M&A?
SS: Well, I think we’re going to see the copper theme continue to play out. Electrification is not going away.
The recent retreat in gold price will, I think, change the market slightly, but the tailwinds are still certainly there, and I think it’s a very constructive time to be in the mining stream.

Vior Gold President and CEO Mathieu Savard (left) chats with The Miner’s Western Editor, Henry Lazenby.
Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 20, 2026
Vior Gold (TSXV: VIO; US-OTC: VIORF) plans to drill 30,000 metres at its Ligneris gold project in Quebec in 2027 to test gaps in the South zone, president and CEO Mathieu Savard says. At Xplor in early November, Savard said Vior still had about 2,000 metres to drill to reach this year’s 30,000-metre target.
At Ligneris, about 600 km northwest of Quebec City and 55 km northwest of Amos, Vior has traced the South zone for more than 1.3 km along strike and intersected gold 845 metres below surface. The company has yet to publish a resource. Savard expects Ligneris to account for about two-thirds of Vior’s 2027 budget.
“We’re still at the early discovery days at Ligneris, so it’s going to take still a while before we can talk about ounces, literally,” Savard told The Northern Miner at Xplor in Montreal. “But we can already see space to drill there and there’s really good indication that we could build ounces fast there.”
Savard wants to find 3 – 5 million oz. to attract a major producer. Vior has the money for next year’s program and wants at least three rigs at Ligneris this winter, when crews can reach some of the harder-to-drill sites.

For True Outdoor Lovers: inTech's Tiny 2027 Flyer Explore Toy Hauler Doesn't Sacrifice Garage Space
18 photos
Photo: inTech RV
Ever since the cart was created, we can say that people have been hitching rides on trailers. In time, and humans being the creative bunch that they are, we would eventually drop walls onto these carts and call them home during long arduous travels.
Fast forward to today, and the beast-drawn carriage and trailer is not so much a common sight, having been replaced with purpose-driven machines that promise to be the solution we look for when traveling away from our rooted homes.
Some travel trailers are aimed at large families that want all the creature comforts possible, while others are aimed at smaller groups that don’t mind an experience that as raw as can be. Come to think of it, these days, we even have countless RV designs that bridge the gap between these extremes.
Photo: inTech RV One style that countless Americans call upon is the toy hauler, trailers which can be used in the traditional sense, to sleep, dine, and share laughs with loved ones, but which also feel very comfortable carrying a couple of dirt bikes, ATVs, rigid kayaks, e-bikes, and even some cars in some cases.
A toy hauler is the reason we’re here today, and unlike other larger ones the market may offer, the 2027 inTech Flyer Explore is actually on the opposite end of the size spectrum and aims to be as compact as possible while still granting us a space where we can go about our daily camping duties and bring along some toys.
Now, the sort of experience that a compact toy hauler can offer is clearly different than a larger one, so don’t expect to see any drop-down beds, massive living areas, or even the largest garage, but there are some very clear reasons why this unit needs to be on your to-consider list.
Photo: inTech RV First and foremost, let’s begin with the garage, an area of the unit that actually occupies almost the entirety of the floorspace, something that is rarely seen in a toy hauler as the sides are usually lined with bedding options, tables and chairs, and more.
The way this is made possible is by the approach inTech took toward designing the Explore. Instead of placing a kitchen inside, inTech chose to move it to the exterior of the RV and hidden and protected in the belly of the camper because it’s placed on a slideout.
This feature slides into the interior countertop construction that hides at the very front of the camper, just in case you’re wondering where it goes. It would have been interesting if the interior countertop could be lifted in order to access the fridge or cooktop inside.
Photo: inTech RV That takes care of the kitchen – the unit has no bathroom – so what about the bedding? The bed we can access in the 2027 Flyer Explore is a fold out bed, but instead of extending into the interior, it actually extends toward the exterior of the unit. This means that you don’t have to park your bike or kayaks outside just to sleep.
Keep in mind that the larger toy haulers out there don’t usually have this ability, and we often need to leave our rides outside in order to accommodate party members in the garage. A big win for inTech I’d say.
Another big win is the fact that inTech advertises this camper with an MSRP of $23,800 (€21,700) in it’s most standard form, and dealers are letting them go for around $25K-$30K depending on features and options added to the mix.
Photo: inTech RV Moving forward with more of the Explore’s magic, allow me to point out that the entire rear wall is actually a gate that drops down and functions as a ramp for you and your gear. When it’s time to pack up, you can lift it with just one hand and lock it into place. Have a look at the clip below to see it in action.
While I can talk you through the features and options that we have inside a Flyer, I’ll leave that to your dealer and instead, tell you a bit about how this camper is made. Clearly, to support the added weight of some toys, it can’t be built out of your typical wood.
Instead, inTech goes to town building the Flyer Explore with an all-aluminum frame and body panels that are also lined with sheets of aluminum on the outside, gelcoat on top and kept in place with the help of some of the most rugged extrusions and seams I’ve seen on a camper of this size and price in a while.
Dry, these babies can weigh as little as 1,580 lbs (717 kg) and can handle nearly double that, or 2,990 lbs (1,456 kg). Maybe if you upgrade the suspension and reinforce the floor, you can push that number higher. Talk things over with a local dealer or get in touch with inTech directly. According to sources, inTech customer service and support is generally viewed as “positive.”
Photo: inTech RV Personally, positive is the feeling I get when looking at this three-season toy hauler, especially since it taps into some neat tricks to grant us access to a space that’s very versatile.
I mean, if it’s not raining and you’re not worried about theft in your camping area, you can easily leave the bikes outside and toss down a couple of sleeping bags where you and your significant other can rest and the kids can take the bed. Why not use the space to set up a dining table? There’s just so much we can do with this much empty floorspace.
These days, travel trailers come in all shapes and sizes, but what the 2027 Flyer Explore brings to the table is versatility in it’s smallest form possible.

Newfoundland and Labrador Prospectors Association President Norm Mercer (left) chats with Northern Miner host Devan Murugan.
By: Northern Miner Staff November 20, 2026
Newfoundland and Labrador should put more money into prospector grants and mentoring as veteran prospectors retire, says Norm Mercer, president of the province’s prospectors association.
Fourteen years after its founding, the Newfoundland and Labrador Prospectors Association raised enough money this year to open an office and hire a part-time geologist, Mercer said early this month at Mineral Resources Review in St. John’s. The group wants to reach young people while they’re still in high school or just starting out in the trades.
“It’s only going to be a small percentage who may go out and make a big discovery, but many could go out and find a mineral property that companies would come and do more work on and option those properties,” Mercer told The Northern Miner .
The first person to receive a provincial prospector’s grant was Al Chislett. In 1993, he and Chris Verbiski were looking for diamonds in Labrador when they spotted a streak of rusty rock from their helicopter. It led them to the nickel, copper and cobalt deposit at Voisey’s Bay.

The US-Built 2027 Subaru Ascent Touring Is a 150-Vehicle Limited Edition in Japan
7 photos
Photo: Subaru
Subaru has decided to bring the Ascent to Japan. The idea came in June 2026, when the manufacturer announced that Indiana-built Ascents may be exported to Subaru's domestic market to leverage a certification system implemented by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport, and Tourism. How come?
You can blame Trump's incredibly polarizing trade policy, prompted by the longstanding US trade deficit with Japan. The prez argued that Japanese regulations and certification requirements made it difficult for American manufacturers to compete in the Japanese market, but truth be told, most American vehicles simply are viewed as subpar by Japanese motorists.
Under a framework agreement that was subsequently implemented through an executive order in September 2025, the lesser partner agreed to make it easier for American-built vehicles to enter its market. Japan changed its certification rules in February 2026, enabling Toyota, Nissan, and Subaru to send a bunch of left-hand-drive American vehicles there, including the Tundra pickup truck.
Toyota and Nissan actually published quality-related warnings on their Japanese websites, acknowledging that US-built models may exhibit both paint and fit-and-finish characteristics that differ from Japanese domestic market automotive quality standards. Ouchie, for sure! Subject vehicles include the aforementioned Toyota Tundra half-ton pickup, the Highlander, and the Nissan Murano.
The Ascent three-row sport utility vehicle is Subaru's first model introduced under the new US-built vehicle certification system. These three Japanese automakers are joined by Honda, which is bringing the Acura Integra Type S and Honda Passport TrailSport Elite to Japanese customers in relatively limited numbers.
Photo: Subaru Limited to 150 vehicles, the Japanese-market Ascent comes in Touring specification with a retail price of 7,700,000 yen. That means 48,460 dollars at current exchange rates, which is less than what you have to pay in the United States of America. For reference, the 2027 model carries an MSRP of $51,165 as of this writing, and that's before destination charge, other taxes, and options.
Only available with seven rather than eight seats, the Ascent Touring is heading to Japan with a bit of a problem. The Japanese website lists a warning that concerns driver-assistance goodies, namely the EyeSight system. Subaru explicitly states that said EyeSight system was developed specifically for right-hand traffic, which is why it may not perform as intended on Japanese roads.
Because it's a seven-seat configuration, the Ascent Touring comes with two individual captain's chairs for the second row instead of a three-person bench seat. Folding both rear rows, the flat cargo floor of the mid-sized crossover extends more than 2 meters (78.7 inches) from the tailgate opening to the front seats, making the 2027 Subaru Ascent Touring useful beyond the school run.
Tipping the scales at 2,060 kilograms (4,542 pounds), the Japanese model carries 73 liters (19.3 gallons) of dinosaur juice in the fuel tank. Its 2.4-liter turbocharged four-cylinder boxer develops 194 kilowatts at 5,600 revolutions per minute and 375 Newton-meters at 2,000 to 4,800 revolutions per minute, figures that can be alternatively read as 260 mechanical ponies and 277 pound-feet.
Brown Nappa leather, 14-speaker Harman Kardon audio, ventilated front seats, Symmetrical All-Wheel Drive, and X-MODE are only a few highlights. This 150-vehicle production run is limited to three paint colors. Crystal White Pearl adds 33,000 yen to the final price, while Magnetite Gray Metallic and Daybreak Blue Pearl are no-cost options. All 150 units are offered through a lottery. View this post on Instagram A post shared by 株式会社SUBARU (@subaru.jp)

Photo: Moment Energy
A retired EV battery can still have years of use left in it when it’s taken off the road. Moment Energy’s new Nova battery storage system puts those packs to work on commercial sites. And when a pack wears out, it can be swapped without pulling out the whole system.
Nova was unveiled at RE+ in Las Vegas this week, and it’s already in production at Megafactory 1, the battery-repurposing plant that Moment Energy opened in the Vancouver area in June.
Each Nova unit delivers 500 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of energy and 200 kilowatts (kW) of power. It has a 2.94 m by 1.80 m (9.7 x 5.9 ft) footprint, and units can be linked together for projects in the tens of megawatt-hours. A site could charge the batteries when electricity is cheaper or when its solar panels are producing more than it needs, then draw on that power when demand spikes or the grid goes down.
Nova can use packs from different EV models, even when those packs have aged at different rates. Moment’s battery management software tracks how each pack is doing. As packs wear out, the company can replace them while leaving the enclosure and concrete pad in place. Moment says its pack replacement service could keep a system in service for more than 20 years.

“We see a future where reengineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chains. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering, and North American manufacturing to deploy the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid,” said Edward Chiang, co-founder and CEO of Moment Energy.
What the safety certifications mean
Moment Energy says Nova is the first storage system built from retired EV batteries to earn both UL 1973 certification for the batteries and UL 9540 certification for the complete system. It was also tested under UL 9540A, which looks at how a battery fire can spread. The factory itself is certified under UL 1974, which covers how used batteries are assessed and graded for reuse.
That matters for businesses with limited space. Nova is designed to sit outdoors alongside the buildings it serves. It uses liquid cooling, detects smoke, heat, and flammable gases, and is rated to operate from −13F to 122F (−25C to 50C).
Moment Energy also says an independent review found that Nova meets US federal sourcing restrictions tied to the clean electricity investment tax credit. Those rules are one part of determining whether a project qualifies for the credit.
Orders are open, and Moment Energy expects the first units to ship in Q1 2027 for deployments across North America.
